Pope Leo has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma after surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. Read the latest Vatican health update, recovery plans, and what is known about his condition.


## Pope Leo Receives Lung Cancer Diagnosis Following Surgery


Pope Leo has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma after undergoing surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, according to a medical bulletin released by the Vatican on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. The procedure was described as successful, with doctors reporting no complications during the operation.


The 71-year-old pontiff underwent surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital after medical examinations identified a growth on his lung. Further tissue testing conducted during the procedure confirmed the suspected diagnosis, providing the first official confirmation of his condition.


The announcement has drawn attention to the pope's health and recovery, particularly as he continues to lead the Catholic Church and manage a demanding schedule of religious duties and international commitments.


According to the Vatican, Pope Leo woke up normally after the operation and was resting in his hospital room following the procedure.


## Details of Pope Leo's Lung Surgery


The operation took place on Tuesday at Gemelli Hospital in Rome, where the pope was admitted earlier in the day. His medical team performed surgery to remove the affected portion of his right lung.


Professor Stefano Margaritora, head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital and the pope's lead surgeon, provided further details in the Vatican's medical update.


The surgical team removed the lower lobe of the right lung using a video-assisted surgical technique. This approach allows doctors to operate with the assistance of a camera and specialised instruments, potentially reducing the need for larger incisions compared with traditional open surgery.


During the procedure, doctors conducted a rapid histological examination of the removed tissue. The results confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, a diagnosis that had already been suspected based on examinations performed before surgery.


The operation lasted approximately 90 minutes. The Vatican reported that it was completed successfully without complications.


Although the initial update was reassuring regarding the immediate outcome of the surgery, the medical bulletin did not provide further details about the cancer's stage, whether it had spread, or whether additional treatment would be necessary.


These details are important for understanding the pope's longer-term outlook, but they remain unconfirmed in the information released by the Vatican.


## What Is Lung Adenocarcinoma?


Lung adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer. It develops in glandular cells that produce substances such as mucus and is one of the most common forms of lung cancer.


The disease can occur in people who smoke as well as those who have never smoked. Its development may be associated with several factors, including age, exposure to certain environmental substances, and genetic changes in lung cells.


Treatment depends on a range of medical factors, including the tumour's size, location, stage, and whether cancer cells have spread beyond the original site.


For some patients whose cancer is detected while it remains localised, surgery to remove the affected lung tissue may be an important part of treatment. Depending on the individual diagnosis, doctors may also consider chemotherapy, targeted medicines, immunotherapy, or other approaches.


However, the specific treatment plan for Pope Leo has not been disclosed in the reported Vatican statement.


The removal of a lung lobe does not, by itself, establish whether a patient's cancer has been completely eliminated. Further pathology findings, imaging results, and clinical assessments may be needed before doctors can determine the next steps.


For that reason, it would be premature to draw conclusions about the pope's prognosis without additional information from his medical team.


## Pope Leo Expected to Remain in Hospital for About a Week


The Vatican previously indicated that Pope Leo was expected to remain at Gemelli Hospital for approximately one week while recovering from surgery.


His public engagements have been cancelled through October 20, allowing time for rest and medical observation.


Before arriving at the hospital, the pope departed the Vatican shortly before 1 p.m. local time. He travelled by car to Gemelli Hospital, located several miles away in Rome.


Upon arrival, Leo greeted several officials and walked past a gathering of well-wishers who had come to show their support. Some called out words of encouragement as he entered the hospital.


The scenes reflected the public interest surrounding the pontiff's health, with Catholics and other observers awaiting further updates on his condition.


Recovery following lung surgery can vary depending on the individual patient's overall health, the extent of the operation, and the body's response to treatment. Medical teams typically monitor breathing, pain, mobility, and other indicators during the initial recovery period.


The Vatican has not announced a detailed rehabilitation timetable or confirmed when Pope Leo will resume his full public schedule.


## Who Is Pope Leo?


Pope Leo, born Robert Prevost in Chicago in 1955, was elected pontiff by the world's cardinals in May 2025. Before becoming pope, he spent decades serving as a missionary, priest, and bishop, including extensive work in Peru.


At 71, he is relatively young compared with some recent leaders of the Catholic Church. He is also known for maintaining an active schedule and has expressed an interest in sports, including tennis.


The reported lung cancer diagnosis is a significant development because the pope's responsibilities involve public appearances, religious ceremonies, meetings with Church leaders, and decisions affecting the global Catholic community.


Unlike many political and institutional leaders, the pope does not have a formal deputy who automatically assumes his position whenever he becomes ill. When a pontiff is temporarily unable to perform his duties, much of the Vatican's administrative work can continue, although matters requiring his personal approval may be delayed.


The Vatican has not indicated that the pope's diagnosis will result in any permanent changes to his responsibilities.


## Pope Leo's Previous Health Experience


Although the pope has not been widely associated with recent health problems, he previously experienced a serious illness during his years of service in Peru.


In 1985, while working as a young priest in Chulucanas, he contracted typhoid fever and required hospital treatment.


He later described the experience in an interview published in a book by Penguin Peru. According to his account, the pain was so severe that he prayed for death rather than continue suffering.


He ultimately recovered and interpreted his survival as a sign that he still had work to do.


The experience formed part of his personal reflections on faith, suffering, and his religious vocation. His current diagnosis represents a different medical challenge, and the details of his recovery will depend on the findings and recommendations of his present medical team.


## Upcoming Travel Plans and Vatican Responsibilities


Before his hospital admission, Pope Leo had a busy schedule of religious and diplomatic commitments.


One major event on his calendar was an 11-day visit to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, scheduled for November 6 to November 17, 2026.


The trip would involve international travel and public engagements, making his recovery timeline particularly relevant.


However, no confirmed decision regarding the tour was included in the reported medical update. Whether the visit proceeds as planned may depend on the pope's progress, medical advice, and the Vatican's assessment of his ability to travel safely.


The health of a pope can have implications beyond his personal schedule because of the Catholic Church's worldwide presence and its approximately 1.4 billion members.


For now, the immediate priority is his recovery from surgery. Further announcements from the Vatican may clarify whether additional treatment is planned and when he will be able to return to his normal duties.


## What Happens Next for Pope Leo?


The immediate medical outlook described in the Vatican's announcement is cautiously encouraging in one important respect: the operation was completed without reported complications, and the pope woke up normally afterward.


Nevertheless, several important questions remain unanswered. These include the precise stage of the cancer, whether the surgical removal achieved clear margins, whether additional treatment will be recommended, and how long his recovery may take.


Such information would help provide a clearer picture of the diagnosis and the medical team's expectations.


Until further details are released, the most reliable approach is to rely on official Vatican communications and verified reporting rather than speculation about the pope's health.


Catholics around the world, along with members of the wider public, will be watching for updates as he recovers at Gemelli Hospital.


## Conclusion


Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosis marks a significant moment for the pontiff and the Catholic Church. Doctors confirmed lung adenocarcinoma after removing the lower lobe of his right lung in a procedure that lasted approximately 90 minutes and was reported to have no complications.


The Vatican expects him to spend about a week in hospital, with public engagements cancelled through October 20. His longer-term treatment plan, cancer stage, and return to international duties have not yet been confirmed in the reported update.


As the pope begins his recovery, further medical information will be essential to understanding his prognosis and the potential impact on his responsibilities.


For now, the confirmed information points to a successful operation, followed by a period of rest and continued medical observation.
